issue.title: F#: option and single-case union columns refused as divergent storage next to plain columns
issue.body:
### Summary

Since #5902, a query that combines an F# `option` / `voption` or single-case-union column with a column that has no
converter (or a different one) fails to translate with "their value converters do not agree on what a stored value
counts", although both columns store the same value.

### Background

#5902 (milestone 6.5.1, not yet released) refuses an operator, a conditional or a set operation between two values
whose value converters differ, because two different conversions make the stored values incommensurable. LinqToDB.FSharp
maps every scalar option and single-case-union member through a value converter, but that converter stores the payload
unchanged: `Some v` is stored as `v` and `None` as `NULL`; `UserId 10` is stored as `10`.

### Current behavior

`SequenceHelper.ConvertTheSameWay` treats "converter vs no converter" and any two converters that are not equal as
divergent, so an option column next to a plain column is refused:

- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/SequenceHelper.cs:60` — `ConvertTheSameWay` returns false when one side has a converter
- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/ExpressionBuildVisitor.cs` — `CombinesDivergentStorage` / `CanShareOneReading` refuse with `Error_ValueConverter_DivergentOperands`
- `Source/LinqToDB.FSharp/FSharpOptionSupport.fs:84`, `Source/LinqToDB.FSharp/FSharpSingleCaseUnionSupport.fs:38` — the converters

```fsharp
type OptRow = { [<PrimaryKey>] Id: int; Age: int option }
db.GetTable<OptRow>().Where(fun x -> x.Age.Value = x.Id)
```

fails on SQLite.MS (direct and remote) with:
`Cannot combine 'Age' and 'Id' in the database: their value converters do not agree on what a stored value counts ...`

The same refusal hits `x.OptKey.Value = x.Key` (`UserId option` vs `UserId`: two different converters) and an
association over an `option` foreign key, whose generated predicate is `x.ParentId.Value == a_Parent.Id` (found by the
scaffold codegen harness for F# scaffolded models).

### Expected behavior

These comparisons translate to plain column comparisons, as before #5902. Converters that actually change the stored
value keep being refused.

### Notes

- Related, separate: #5886 (an option `.Value` compared with a literal passes the unconverted element as a parameter).
- Reproduced and fixed on the #5707 branch; the fix will be its own PR on top of master.

issue.title: SQLite: string.Join over object items concatenates an arithmetic item without parentheses
issue.body:
### Summary

On SQLite, `string.Join` over `object` items renders an arithmetic item as a bare operand of `||`. SQLite binds `||` tighter than `+`, so the rest of the joined string is added to the item's last operand, and the result is a number.

### Background

SQLite lists `||` above `* / %` and `+ -` in its operator table, "listed in precedence order (top to bottom / highest to lowest)": https://www.sqlite.org/lang_expr.html#operators

### Current behavior

```cs
[Table]
sealed class JoinProbeEntity
{
	[PrimaryKey] public int Id     { get; set; }
	[Column]     public int Value1 { get; set; }
}

using var db    = GetDataContext(context); // SQLite.Classic or SQLite.MS
using var table = db.CreateLocalTable(new[] { new JoinProbeEntity { Id = 1, Value1 = 10 } });

table.Select(e => string.Join(",", new object[] { e.Value1 + 1, e.Value1 })).ToArray();
// expected: "11,10"
// actual:   "11"
```

```sql
SELECT
	[e].[Value1] + 1 || ',' || [e].[Value1]
FROM
	[JoinProbeEntity] [e]
```

SQLite evaluates it as `[e].[Value1] + (1 || ',' || [e].[Value1])`, i.e. `10 + '1,10'`, which is `11`.

- `Source/LinqToDB/SqlQuery/Precedence.cs:16-23` — `Concatenate = 5`, below every other operator. The comment describes it as defensive: a concat nested in another operator gets parentheses. The reverse case, an arithmetic operand inside a concat, is left bare, which changes the result wherever `||` binds tighter than `+`.
- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/DataProvider/SQLite/Translation/SQLiteMemberTranslator.cs:281-346` — SQLite's `TranslateStringJoin`; an inline array goes through `ConfigureConcatWsEmulation` (`:334`).

`string.Concat(new object[] { ... })` over the same items is correct: it casts each item (`CAST([e].[Value1] + 1 AS NVarChar(11))`), which keeps the arithmetic inside the cast.

### Expected behavior

`"11,10"`: the arithmetic item parenthesized (`([e].[Value1] + 1) || ','`) or converted to text the way `string.Concat` does it.

### Notes

- Related: #5527 (the precedence table is provider-agnostic). This is a wrong-result case rather than redundant brackets.
- Found while writing tests for #5932, but independent of it: it reproduces without any outer join, and `Precedence.cs` and `Internal/DataProvider/SQLite` are unchanged between master `7c5d5b5ae8` and that branch.
- Not checked on other providers. Not pinned: why the `string.Join` item path emits no cast where `string.Concat` does.

issue.title: IndexExpression in a query tree throws NotSupportedException from PathVisitor
issue.body:
### Summary

A query whose expression tree contains an `IndexExpression` (`ExpressionType.Index`) fails with `NotSupportedException: Unhandled expression type: Index` before any translation happens. Hand-built trees are the only way to produce one, so this affects callers that construct predicates programmatically — rules engines, dynamic-LINQ layers, non-C# front ends.

### Background

The C# compiler never emits `IndexExpression` when it lowers an expression-tree lambda: `values[0]` over an array becomes a `BinaryExpression` with `NodeType` `ArrayIndex`, `list[0]` becomes a `MethodCallExpression` on the indexer's getter, and a multi-dimensional array read becomes a `MethodCallExpression` on `Array.Get`. `IndexExpression` appears only when something calls `Expression.ArrayAccess`, `Expression.MakeIndex`, or `Expression.Property(obj, indexer, args)` directly. That is why the gap has gone unnoticed — nothing in the repository constructs one, and no C# query can.

### Current behavior

`PathVisitor.Path` switches on `expr.NodeType` and throws for anything it does not recognise. There is no `ExpressionType.Index` case:

- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Expressions/ExpressionVisitors/PathVisitor.cs:265` — `throw new NotSupportedException($"Unhandled expression type: {expr.NodeType}")`

The visitor runs over the whole query expression from `ExpressionCacheManager`'s constructor, which every query passes through:

- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/ExpressionCacheManager.cs:51` — `mainExpression.GetExpressionAccessors(...)`
- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Expressions/InternalExtensions.cs:188` — `GetExpressionAccessors`

so the failure lands at the entrance to `ParametersContext`, long before provider translation.

Reproduced on `SQLite.Classic` / net10.0:

```csharp
var values = new[] { "str", "str1" };

Expression<Func<string[]>> captured = () => values;

var entity    = Expression.Parameter(typeof(ParameterDeduplication), "t");
var predicate = Expression.Lambda<Func<ParameterDeduplication, bool>>(
    Expression.Equal(
        Expression.Property(entity, nameof(ParameterDeduplication.String2)),
        Expression.ArrayAccess(captured.Body, Expression.Constant(0))),
    entity);

db.GetTable<ParameterDeduplication>().Where(predicate).ToSqlQuery();
```

```
System.NotSupportedException : Unhandled expression type: Index
   at PathVisitor`1.Path(Expression expr) in PathVisitor.cs:265
   ...
   at InternalExtensions.GetExpressionAccessors(Expression expression, Expression path)
   at ExpressionCacheManager..ctor(Expression mainExpression, IUniqueIdGenerator`1 generator) in ExpressionCacheManager.cs:51
   at ParametersContext..ctor(IQueryExpressions parametersExpression, ExpressionTreeOptimizationContext optimizationContext, IDataContext dataContext) in ParametersContext.cs:28
```

### Expected behavior

`PathVisitor` handles `ExpressionType.Index` the way it handles the shapes it already supports — walking `IndexExpression.Object` and `IndexExpression.Arguments` — so a tree carrying one is translated rather than rejected. An array access built with `Expression.ArrayAccess` should behave the same as the `ArrayIndex` binary the compiler emits for the same source.

### Notes

`ExpressionEqualityComparer` and `ExpressionPrinter` already handle the node (`ExpressionEqualityComparer.cs:268,436`, `ExpressionPrinter.cs:332,1019`), so `PathVisitor` looks like the only gap on this path. That is not confirmed beyond it, though: the throw happens first, so whether the rest of the pipeline copes once the node is let through is unverified.

This also makes an arm of `ExpressionCacheManager.SuggestParameterDisplayName` unreachable. #5740 adds

```csharp
IndexExpression { Object: { } target } =>
    SuggestParameterDisplayName(target),
```

which no input can reach while this throw stands. The regression test for it is committed on that PR, gated on this issue.

issue.title: `SocketException` after upgrading `linq2db.EntityFrameworkCore` to ≥9.1.0
issue.body:
### Description

Starting with `linq2db.EntityFrameworkCore` ≥9.1.0 , `DatabaseFacade.EnsureCreatedAsync()` is throwing a `SocketException` after `LinqToDBForEFTools.CreateLinqToDBConnection()` has been called:
```cs
using (var dataConnection = dbContext.CreateLinqToDBConnection())
{
    // ...
}

await dbContext.Database.EnsureDeletedAsync();
await dbContext.Database.EnsureCreatedAsync(); // SocketException: An established connection was aborted by the software in your host machine
```

### Reproduction Steps

Install the following packages:
```xml
<PackageReference Include="linq2db" Version="6.1.0" />
<PackageReference Include="linq2db.EntityFrameworkCore" Version="10.1.0" />
<PackageReference Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore" Version="10.0.1" />
```

```cs
using LinqToDB;

    .WithDatabase("pwprdb")
    .WithUsername("postgres")
    .WithPassword("postgres")
    .Build();

await dbContainer.StartAsync();
```

issue.title: Query cache ignores closure state in a `LoadWith` filter lambda, so the first call's eager-load SQL is reused
PostgreSQL: provider-specific BulkCopy applies BulkCopyTimeout to the first batch only
issue.body:
### Summary

With `BulkCopyType.ProviderSpecific`, the PostgreSQL provider applies `BulkCopyTimeout` only to the first `COPY` batch. Every later batch runs under the connection's command timeout, so e.g. `BulkCopyTimeout = 0` (infinite) stops holding once the row count exceeds one batch.

### Current behavior

`PostgreSQLBulkCopy` splits the source into batches of `Math.Max(10, MaxBatchSize ?? 10000)` rows and opens a new `NpgsqlBinaryImporter` for each batch. `ConfigureWriter` (which sets `Timeout` from `BulkCopyTimeout`) is called only for the first importer; the importer re-created when a batch fills is never configured. Npgsql's importer sets no timeout of its own, so it falls back to the connection's `Command Timeout`.

The same pattern is in all three paths (line numbers from master `7c5d5b5ae`):

- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/DataProvider/PostgreSQL/PostgreSQLBulkCopy.cs:113-115` — first writer configured; `:213` — `ProviderSpecificCopySyncImpl` re-creates the writer without `ConfigureWriter`
- `:277-281` / `:340-342` — same for `ProviderSpecificCopyImplAsync(..., IEnumerable<T>, ...)`
- `:398-402` / `:464-466` — same for `ProviderSpecificCopyImplAsync(..., IAsyncEnumerable<T>, ...)`

Present in 6.4.0, 6.5.0 and master.

### Reproduction

```sql
CREATE TABLE probe_t (id int NOT NULL, v text);
CREATE FUNCTION probe_slow() RETURNS trigger LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN PERFORM pg_sleep(4); RETURN NULL; END $$;
CREATE TRIGGER probe_slow_trg AFTER INSERT ON probe_t FOR EACH STATEMENT EXECUTE FUNCTION probe_slow();
```

Connection string with `Command Timeout=2`:

```csharp
var opts = new BulkCopyOptions { BulkCopyType = BulkCopyType.ProviderSpecific, BulkCopyTimeout = 0, MaxBatchSize = 10 };
await db.BulkCopyAsync(opts, Enumerable.Range(1, N).Select(i => new ProbeRow { Id = i, V = "x" }).ToList());
```

- N = 5 (one `COPY`): succeeds after ~6.5 s — the timeout of 0 is honoured.
- N = 25 (three `COPY`s): fails after ~6.4 s with `NpgsqlException: Exception while reading from stream` → `TimeoutException: Timeout during reading attempt`. The first `COPY` passes; the second times out 2 s later.

Also reproduced on PostgreSQL 18 / Npgsql 10 in sync, async-`IEnumerable` and async-`IAsyncEnumerable` modes (1.5 s trigger sleep, `Command Timeout=1`, 15 rows): all three fail with the exception above; the 5-row single-batch case passes.

### Expected behavior

Every batch's importer gets the same timeout configuration as the first one, so `BulkCopyTimeout` applies to the whole bulk copy regardless of row count. With `BulkCopyTimeout = null` and `BulkCopyUseConnectionCommandTimeout = false`, importers stay unconfigured, as today.

### Notes

- The timeout support was added in #5377 (for #5357); the per-batch re-creation was not covered there.
- Other providers are not affected.

issue.title: Firebird: char literal ' is emitted as ''' (invalid SQL)
issue.body:
### Summary

A `char` value `'` written as a SQL literal on Firebird is emitted as `'''`, which is an unterminated string literal, instead of `''''`.

### Current behavior

`Source/LinqToDB/Internal/DataProvider/Firebird/FirebirdMappingSchema.cs:183-194` — `ConvertCharToSql`:

```csharp
stringBuilder
	.Append('\'')
	.Append(value == '\'' ? '\'' : value)
	.Append('\'');
```

Both branches of the conditional append a single quote, so the apostrophe is never doubled. The `string` converter in the same file escapes correctly (`:164`, `value.Replace("'", "''", StringComparison.Ordinal)`); MySQL has the intended `char` form (`MySqlMappingSchema.cs:86`, `if (value == '\'') stringBuilder.Append("''")`).

Generated SQL (`FirebirdVersion.v5`, via `ToSqlQuery()`):

```csharp
db.GetTable<T>().Where(x => x.Ch == '\'')
// SELECT ... WHERE "x"."Ch" = '''

db.InlineParameters = true;
var ch = '\'';
db.GetTable<T>().Where(x => x.Ch == ch)
// SELECT ... WHERE "x"."Ch" = '''
```

A `string` constant `"'"` in the same query shape produces the correct `''''`.

### Expected behavior

```sql
SELECT ... WHERE "x"."Ch" = ''''
```

i.e. append `''` when `value == '\''`, `value` otherwise.

### Notes

- Reproduced on master (89b5ce162) by SQL generation only; not executed against a live Firebird server.
- The `IsLiteralEncodingSupported` UTF-8 path (`_utf8 x'..'`) only handles characters that need encoding, so an ASCII `'` always goes through the broken branch.
- Other paths that write `char` values as literals (e.g. `BulkCopyType.MultipleRows`) are expected to be affected the same way but were not checked.
- The conditional dates from 4aebf4395 (2017).

issue.title: Remote context: server ignores configuration-scoped column attributes
issue.body:
### Summary

On a remote context (`LinqService`), the server ignores configuration-scoped mapping attributes on columns. It re-resolves every deserialized column against a mapping schema that carries no provider configuration, so `[Column(Configuration = …)]` never matches and the unscoped attribute wins. A direct context over the same provider resolves the scoped one.

### Current behavior

- `Source/LinqToDB/Remote/LinqService.cs:114, 146, 209, 244-245`: each operation creates the per-request `db` through `CreateDataContext(configuration)`, then deserializes the query with `LinqServiceSerializer.Deserialize(SerializationMappingSchema, MappingSchema ?? SerializationMappingSchema, db.Options, …)`. The context schema passed is the service's own `MappingSchema` (often `null`) or the bare `SerializationMappingSchema`, not `db.MappingSchema`.
- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Remote/LinqServiceSerializer.cs:2121-2129`: for each `SqlField` of a `SqlTable` with an `ObjectType`, the deserializer sets `field.ColumnDescriptor = _contextSchema.GetEntityDescriptor(sqlTable.ObjectType, …)[field.Name]`.
- `Source/LinqToDB/Mapping/MappingSchema.cs:1225-1236`: attributes are filtered by the schema's `ConfigurationList`. That schema's list contains no provider configuration, so scoped attributes are dropped.

The client side resolves correctly. For

```cs
[Column(DataType = DataType.DateTime2, Precision = 3)]
[Column(Configuration = ProviderName.ClickHouse)]
public DateTime Wide { get; set; }
```

both `ClickHouse.Octonica` and the `ClickHouse.Octonica.LinqService` client report the configuration list `[…, ClickHouse.Octonica, ClickHouse]` and the column type `DateTime64(7)`. The server nevertheless writes the insert literal as `toDateTime64('…', 3)`, taken from the unscoped attribute, while the direct context writes `toDateTime64('…', 7)`.

### Expected behavior

The server resolves columns against the per-request context's mapping schema, so remote and direct contexts produce the same SQL and store the same data. `CreateDataContext` already adds the service's `MappingSchema` to that context (`LinqService.cs:67-68`), so nothing the current argument provides is lost.

Measured on ClickHouse.Octonica: a value written as `10:11:12.1234567` through that column reads back as `10:11:12.1234567` from the direct context and as `10:11:12.1230000` from the remote one.

### Notes

- Passing `db.MappingSchema` makes the remote read-back match direct, and makes the five ClickHouse remote tests from #5959 that tripped the baseline check pass. That was verified locally before the change was put on its own branch.
- Where the server actually uses the re-resolved descriptor has only been observed on the ClickHouse insert path. On SQLite, inserts (parameter and inline), an inline update, an inline `WHERE` and Guid inserts produced the same SQL and data on both sides, because the value types are already fixed on the client for those shapes.
- Found while widening the #5959 tests. They surfaced as *Baselines for remote context doesn't match direct access baselines* on the ClickHouse remote contexts (#5965 lists the symptom).
- The impact is not only on SQL text: a remote insert through a scoped attribute can store different data than a direct one (above, precision 3 truncates sub-millisecond ticks). Anything else the server reads from the column descriptor is exposed the same way.

issue.title: PostgreSQL: netstandard2.0 build can't read Npgsql 10 date/time/daterange into DateTime/TimeSpan/NpgsqlRange<DateTime>
issue.body:
### Description

Npgsql 10 returns `DateOnly` for `date`, `TimeOnly` for `time` and `NpgsqlRange<DateOnly>` for `daterange`. The net8+ build of linq2db converts those to the classic `DateTime` / `TimeSpan` / `NpgsqlRange<DateTime>` property types. That conversion lives under `SUPPORTS_DATEONLY` (`PostgreSQLDataProvider.cs:88-93`, `PostgreSQLMappingSchema.cs:75-82`), so the **netstandard2.0** build has none of it. An app on a modern runtime that loads the ns2.0 asset fails on a plain `DateTime` property:

```
LinqToDB.Common.LinqToDBConvertException : Cannot convert value '12/12/2012: System.DateOnly' to type 'System.DateTime'
LinqToDB.Common.LinqToDBConvertException : Cannot convert value '12:12: System.TimeOnly' to type 'System.TimeSpan'
LinqToDB.Common.LinqToDBConvertException : Cannot convert value '[2/3/2000,3/4/2000): NpgsqlTypes.NpgsqlRange`1[System.DateOnly]' to type 'NpgsqlTypes.NpgsqlRange`1[System.DateTime]'
```

The ns2.0 asset runs on modern runtimes through a netstandard2.0 library, and for every app whose runtime's TFM is dropped (net8/net9 next). Every PostgreSQL user on Npgsql 10 reading a `date` column into `DateTime` would hit this. Same class as #6067.

Locally (`worktree-test.ps1 -LinqToDBAsset netstandard2.0`, PostgreSQL 18), these are red on the ns2.0 code paths and green on net10.0: `PostgreSQLTests.TestDate`, `TestRange`, `TestRangeBulkCopy` and `TestRangeBulkCopyAsync`. `TestTableFunction` is also red there on `time` → `TimeSpan`; on net10.0 it fails later, on an unrelated pre-existing error.

### Proposed fix

Register the `DateOnly`/`TimeOnly` → `DateTime`/`TimeSpan` (and range) conversions on every TFM, resolving the types at runtime (`Type.GetType("System.DateOnly")`) and building the converters by reflection. Out of scope: mapping `DateOnly`/`TimeOnly` *properties* on the ns2.0 build, which is a separate feature.

issue.title: Internal analyzer: flag unsatisfiable ProjectFlags conjunctions
issue.body:
### Summary

`ProjectFlags` combines a mutually-exclusive build purpose with independent modifier flags, but nothing enforces that split. A conjunction that can never be true — most recently `flags.IsKeys() && flags.IsExpand()` — compiles cleanly, passes every test, and silently guards dead code. An internal analyzer over `Source/LinqToDB` would turn that into a build error.

### Background

`ProjectFlags` values reaching `IBuildContext.MakeExpression` are produced in exactly one place: `ExpressionBuildVisitor.GetProjectFlags` (`Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/ExpressionBuildVisitor.cs:495`). It switches on a single `_buildPurpose` and adds one base flag per arm, then optionally adds `MemberRoot` and `ForSetProjection`. `Keys` is added only in the `Sql`, `Expression` and `Extract` arms.

That yields two invariants:

| Kind | Flags | Constraint |
|---|---|---|
| Purpose | `Root`, `AggregationRoot`, `AssociationRoot`, `SQL`, `Expression`, `Table`, `Traverse`, `Subquery`, `ExtractProjection`, `Expand` | exactly one is set |
| Modifier | `Keys`, `MemberRoot`, `ForSetProjection` | independent, except `Keys` only accompanies `SQL` / `Expression` / `ExtractProjection` |

Neither is expressible in the type system today, and `ProjectFlagExtensions` exposes a flat `Is*()` predicate per flag, so any pair reads as equally plausible. `IsSqlOrExpression()` (`ProjectFlagExtensions.cs:52`) already encodes one of these exclusions by hand, which shows the model is understood but not enforced.

### Current behavior

Three sites reason about the `Keys` / `Expand` pair, and none of the conditions can be true as written:

- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/TableBuilder.TableContext.cs:215` — `if (flags.IsExpand() && !flags.IsKeys())`. The `!IsKeys()` clause is always true, so the condition is just `IsExpand()`.
- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/SelectContext.cs:89` — the same `(flags.IsExpand() && !flags.IsKeys())` sub-clause, likewise redundant.
- PR #5727 added `if (flags.IsKeys() && flags.IsExpand())` guarding 43 lines in `EntityConstructorBase.BuildFullEntityExpressionInternal`. The condition is unsatisfiable, so the block never ran.

The third case passed four automated review passes and a fully green `test-all`. It was identified only by instrumenting the call site: across the whole `EagerLoadingTests` fixture on SQLite, 1621 calls reached that method in six distinct combinations — `SQL`, `Expression`, `SQL+Keys`, `SQL+MemberRoot`, `Expression+ForSetProjection`, `SQL+Keys+MemberRoot`. `Expand` never appeared at all.

The two redundant guards are harmless on their own, but they make the invalid pattern look idiomatic, which is a plausible route to how the dead branch came to be written.

### Expected behavior

An internal analyzer in `Source/CodeGenerators` — alongside `SqlBuilderAliasAnalyzer` / `LINQ2DB0001`, referenced with `OutputItemType="Analyzer"` and shipped in no package — reports:

- a conjunction of two purpose predicates, or of `IsKeys()` with a purpose outside `SQL` / `Expression` / `ExtractProjection`, as **always false** (the guarded code is unreachable);
- a negated-modifier clause that is always true, such as `!IsKeys()` under `IsExpand()`, as **redundant**.

Both `Is*()` extension calls and direct `HasFlag` / bitmask forms should be recognised.

This is deliberately not a user-facing rule: `ProjectFlags` is internal and the invariant is meaningless outside the query builder, so `Source/LinqToDB.Analyzers` (the shipped `L2DB1xxx` package) is the wrong host.

### Notes

- **Drift risk.** The analyzer's exclusion table would be derived from `GetProjectFlags` but not linked to it, so adding `Keys` to the `Expand` arm would make the analyzer wrong. Suggested mitigation: a unit test enumerating `GetProjectFlags` over every (`_buildPurpose` × `BuildFlags`) pair and pinning the produced set, so a model change reddens a test that points at the analyzer. That test is worth having on its own — the reachable flag set is documented nowhere and had to be recovered empirically.
- **Alternative considered, rejected for now.** Splitting the purpose out of `ProjectFlags` into its own enum field would make the impossible states unrepresentable and need no analyzer. It touches every `MakeExpression` implementation and the whole flag-threading path, so the blast radius is far larger than the defect warrants.
- The two redundant guards above are pre-existing and independent of #5727; they can be cleaned up when the rule lands.
- Related: #5788 proposes analyzers for a structurally similar gap — an invariant applied by hand and verified by nothing.

issue.title: "Coalesce used with type that cannot be null" when a struct built in an inner projection is referenced twice
issue.body:
### Description

When an inner projection (chained `Select`, `Concat`/`Union`, subquery) constructs a value-type object (struct) and the outer projection references that member two or more times, query building throws `InvalidOperationException: Coalesce used with type that cannot be null`.

`FinalizeExpressionVisitor.VisitSqlGenericConstructorExpression` memoizes a constructor it sees more than once as `variable = variable ?? constructed`, with `variable` typed as the constructed type. For a non-nullable struct, `Expression.Coalesce` rejects the left operand.

Referencing the struct once works. So does constructing it twice directly in one `Select` over a table, because that never becomes a duplicated `SqlGenericConstructorExpression`.

### Reproduction Steps

```cs
readonly record struct ParentValue(int Id, int? Value);

// chained Select
db.Parent
	.Select(p => new { p.ParentID, Info = new ParentValue(p.ParentID, p.Value1) })
	.Select(m => new { First = m.Info, Second = m.Info })
	.ToList();

// Concat
db.Parent.Where(p => p.ParentID < 4)
	.Select(p => new { p.ParentID, Info = new ParentValue(p.ParentID, p.Value1) })
	.Concat(db.Parent.Where(p => p.ParentID >= 4)
		.Select(p => new { p.ParentID, Info = new ParentValue(p.ParentID, p.Value1) }))
	.Select(m => new { First = m.Info, Second = m.Info })
	.ToList();

// Concat, struct passed into both branches of a conditional
abstract record ValueHolder(ParentValue Info);
sealed record LowHolder(ParentValue Info)  : ValueHolder(Info);
sealed record HighHolder(ParentValue Info) : ValueHolder(Info);

/* same Concat */
	.Select(m => m.ParentID < 4 ? new LowHolder(m.Info) : (ValueHolder)new HighHolder(m.Info))
	.ToList();
```

All three throw. Expected: the rows are returned.

issue.title: Recursive CTE drops columns when recursive term projects a differing-but-assignable type
issue.body:
### Summary

A recursive CTE built with `GetCte<T>(anchor.Concat(recursive))` drops columns when the
recursive term's projection constructs a different-but-assignable type (a polymorphic /
base-cast projection) than the anchor term. The dropped columns are the ones used only in
the recursive self-join and the outer join, so the emitted SQL is malformed (SQLite:
`circular reference: partHierarchy`; other providers: invalid/missing column). This is the
same class of column-tracking loss as #5457, for a query shape that #5680's fix does not cover.

### Background

Set-operation projection merging represents the two operand projections as a conditional
`test ? proj1 : proj2`. When the two projections have differing-but-assignable static types,
`SetOperationBuilder.MakeCondition` wraps one branch in `Expression.Convert` to unify the type.

### Current behavior

- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/SetOperationBuilder.cs:244` — `MakeCondition`
  Convert-wraps a branch when `ifTrue.Type != ifFalse.Type`, yielding
  `test ? BaseCtor : Convert(DerivedCtor)`.
- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/BuildProxyBase{TOwner}.cs:238` (master) —
  `ProcessTranslated` has no `ConditionalExpression` case, so the merged conditional falls
  through to the generic `BuildProxyVisitor`, losing the per-member tracking path; the
  recursive-CTE fields register with a null path and the unresolved columns are pruned.
  (PR #5680 adds a `ConditionalExpression` case — on its branch, unmerged — but it matches
  only when *both* branches are bare `SqlGenericConstructorExpression`, so a Convert-wrapped
  branch still falls through.)

The emitted SQL declares the CTE with only a subset of columns while the recursive branch
references a pruned one — SQLite rejects it with `SQLite Error 1: 'circular reference: partHierarchy'`.

### Expected behavior

Columns used only in the recursive/outer joins must survive regardless of whether the two
set-operation branches share the exact same projected type. A recursive CTE whose recursive
term projects a derived type (cast to the CTE type) should generate the same well-formed SQL
as one whose terms share the exact type.

### Notes

- Related: #5457 (same column-drop class, same-type case) and its fix PR #5680. This gap was
  surfaced while reviewing #5680. Verified pre-existing: the repro fails **identically** on
  `master` and on #5680's branch, so it is **not** introduced by #5680.
- Suggested fix (unverified): in the `ConditionalExpression` case #5680 adds to
  `ProcessTranslated`, unwrap a `Convert`/`ConvertChecked` around each branch before matching,
  then re-wrap after propagating the member path. Needs its own regression tests.
- Repro (fails on SQLite; recursive-CTE providers generally):

```csharp
sealed class Part      { [PrimaryKey] public int Id { get; set; } public string? Name { get; set; } }
sealed class Reference { [PrimaryKey] public int Id { get; set; } public int ParentId { get; set; } public int ReferenceId { get; set; } }
class        CteBase   { public object? RootPartSortField { get; set; } public int RootPartId { get; set; } public int PartId { get; set; } public int HierarchyLevel { get; set; } }
sealed class CteDerived : CteBase { }

var anchor = parts
    .Select(x => new CteBase { RootPartSortField = x.Name, RootPartId = x.Id, HierarchyLevel = 0, PartId = x.Id })
    .OrderBy(x => x.RootPartSortField).Skip(0).Take(20);

var partCte = db.GetCte<CteBase>(h =>
    anchor.Concat(
        h.InnerJoin(refs, (cte, r) => r.ParentId == cte.PartId,
            // recursive term projects a DERIVED type cast to the CTE type -> Convert-wrapped branch
            (cte, r) => (CteBase)new CteDerived { RootPartSortField = cte.RootPartSortField, RootPartId = cte.RootPartId, PartId = r.ReferenceId, HierarchyLevel = cte.HierarchyLevel + 1 })));

var result = parts.InnerJoin(partCte, (me, cte) => me.Id == cte.PartId, (me, id) => new { id.RootPartId, me }).ToList();
// throws: SQLite Error 1: 'circular reference: partHierarchy'
```

issue.body:
### Description

After upgrading from latest 5.x (EFCore 9) to 6.4.0 (EFCore 10), I ran into an issue with BulkCopy (but it's more general than that).
The issue is unhidden if **1 DbContext type** is **reused with different providers** (eg. SQLite and MSSql) **in the same process**.

`MappingSchema` is cached by a key generated by `ModelCacheKeyFactory` which uses `ModelCacheKey` which takes only the type(!) of the DbContext as the caching key (+1 one irrelevant one).

This causes issues, if - like we - have 2 categories of integration tests in 1 test project which therefore run in 1 process: one fast one with SQLite, and one with the acutally used database provider for MSSql.

### Current Behavior
✅ If I only run SQLite tests, they work.
✅ If I only run MSSql tests, they work.
❌ If I **run _both_**, the the **_first discovered_ model wins**. Any differences (in our case `timestamp`) will fail on the other provider.

Eg. an `EntityTypeConfiguration` for supporting both MSSql Server and SQLite:
```csharp
if (_database.IsSqlServer())
{
    builder.Property(e => e.Timestamp)
        .IsRowVersion()
        .IsConcurrencyToken()
        .HasColumnName("timestamp");
}
else
{
    builder.Property(e => e.Timestamp)
        .IsRequired(false);
}
```

### Expected Behavior
The **provider type** should also be **part of the caching key** (see. `Linq2DBForEFTools._mappingSchemas`, especially `GetMappingSchema(...)`).

This should help avoid conflicting provider MappingSchemas due to slightly different models.

### Workaround
(Yet untested) Inherit from the real DbContext to force a seperate MappingSchema key.

### Reproduction Steps

- Add mentioned provider packages
- Add a test file which uses SQLite EF Core provider with real DbContext
  - Let the test insert an entity with a column which is differently mapped/handled per provider (difference should cause an error if the other provider consumes it, like a column db-generated in one but not the other, see below)

issue.title: JoinsOptimizer throws "Cannot get field for SqlFunction" when removing a left join onto a grouping with a computed key
DB2: AllTypes table accumulates junk rows across test runs (ResetAllTypesIdentity never deletes on DB2)
issue.body:
## Problem

`AllTypes` on DB2 accumulates rows that are never cleaned up. `ResetAllTypesIdentity`'s DB2 branch (`Tests/Base/TestBase.Identity.cs`) only reseeds the identity counter (`RESTART WITH 3`) — it never deletes rows, unlike the Informix branch, which has an explicit `DELETE FROM AllTypes WHERE ID > lastValue`. The class-level comment documents this as intentional:

> We intentionally don't remove extra records and allow it to fail in that cases to allow us detect tests that forget to cleanup and leave junk records in those tables

So a leftover row is meant to surface as a test failure (typically via an identity/row-selection mismatch), pointing at whichever test forgot to clean up after itself.

## Evidence

CI build [22698](https://dev.azure.com/linq2db/linq2db/_build/results?buildId=22698) (commit 5b6fcaaf9) failed `DataProviderTests.TestDataTypes("DB2")`'s `TestType` assertions with rows at IDs far above the expected 1/2:

```
Assert.That(id, Is.EqualTo(2))   Expected: 2   But was: 183642
Assert.That(id, Is.EqualTo(2))   Expected: 2   But was:  83641
Assert.That(id, Is.EqualTo(1))   Expected: 1   But was:  50773   (x4)
Assert.That(id, Is.EqualTo(1))   Expected: 1   But was: 182126
Assert.That(id, Is.EqualTo(1))   Expected: 1   But was: 216310
```

At least five distinct surviving IDs up to 216310 — `AllTypes` on DB2 had accumulated roughly 216k inserts' worth of rows never cleaned up. This is a real leak somewhere in the DB2 test path, not one isolated leftover row colliding with a magic number.

(Surfaced via [#5754](https://github.com/linq2db/linq2db/pull/5754), which added `ORDER BY ID` to `DataProviderTestBase.PassNullSql`/`PassValueSql` — see that PR's discussion for the review thread this issue was split out of. The `ORDER BY` change itself is a separate, independent fix for non-deterministic row selection and is not reverted by this issue; it's tracked here because silencing the symptom removes the only signal that was catching this leak.)

## What's needed

1. Identify the test (or tests) that insert into the shared `AllTypes` table on DB2 without cleaning up — the accumulation is large enough (~216k rows) that it's plausibly a single high-iteration or repeatedly-run test/fixture rather than a one-off leftover.
2. Consider adding an explicit `COUNT(*)` / `MAX(ID)` sanity assertion on `AllTypes` in fixture setup (suggested in the #5754 review thread), so a future recurrence fails deterministically and immediately, rather than depending on which row the optimizer happens to pick without `ORDER BY`.
3. Once the leaking test is fixed, DB2's `ResetAllTypesIdentity` could optionally gain the same explicit `DELETE FROM AllTypes WHERE ID > lastValue` the Informix branch already has, if leaving no ambiguity is preferred over the current detect-via-failure design.

## Environment

- Provider: DB2 LUW 11.5
- Surfaced under both CI (`test-all`) and local parallel test runs; not yet confirmed whether reproduction requires parallel execution against the shared DB2 container or also occurs sequentially.

issue.title: Test progress heartbeat: report the filtered test count as total under --filter
issue.body:
### Summary

Under `--filter`, the `--test-progress` heartbeat reports the discovered test count as `total`, not the number of tests the filter selects. `total`, the percentage and `etaSec` are therefore wrong by orders of magnitude on every filtered run, which is the common local case.

### Current behavior

- `Tests/Base/TestProgressReporter.cs:72-74`: on the root suite, `TestProgressTracker.OnBefore` calls `_state.SetTotal(test.TestCaseCount)`. The comment there acknowledges it: *"under a --filter this is the discovered (pre-filter) count, so it over-counts."*
- `etaSec` is computed from that total (`Write`, same file), so it inherits the error.
- `.claude/scripts/test-status.ps1:71-79` relays `total` verbatim as `completed/total (pct%)`.

Observed: a run of 14 test methods x 7 providers (`--filter` of 14 `FullyQualifiedName~` terms plus `CreateData.CreateDatabase`, net10.0) reported `"total": 70328` and `"etaSec": 515501` after 20 tests had started. This reads as a runaway full-suite run and prompts cancelling a correctly scoped one.

### Expected behavior

`total` is the number of tests the run will actually execute under the given `--filter`, e.g. roughly `14 x <contexts>` for the run above, and the ETA is derived from that.

A possible approach:

- The tracker reads the `--filter` value from the process arguments, the same way `TestCommandLine` already reads `--provider` / `--test-progress`.
- On the root suite, it walks the test tree once and counts the leaf tests that match the filter, using a small evaluator for the VSTest filter syntax the repo tooling emits: `FullyQualifiedName` with `~`, `=`, `!=`, `!~`, combined with `|`, `&`, `!` and parentheses.
- With no `--filter`, behavior is unchanged.

### Notes

- The NUnit `ITestAction` does not see the filter the adapter applies, which is why the evaluation has to happen in the tracker.
- Matching must use the same name the adapter maps `FullyQualifiedName` to for parameterized cases (`TestName("provider")`), or the count drifts from what actually runs. A test that compares the computed total with the completed count at the end of a filtered run would catch that.
- For filter properties the evaluator does not support (`TestCategory`, `Name`, ...), a safe fallback is to keep the discovered count and mark it as an upper bound (e.g. `totalIsUpperBound: true`), with `test-status.ps1` then showing `completed/?` and no ETA, rather than guessing.
- `.claude/docs/testing.md` → *Monitoring a long run* should drop any caveat about the over-count once this lands.

issue.title: Investigate removing the explicit PreLoadSQLite_BaseDirectory configuration
issue.body:
`PreLoadSQLite_BaseDirectory` is set in three places and there is strong evidence nothing reads it. It looks like a leftover from the System.Data.SQLite **1.x** line, which loaded `SQLite.Interop.dll` and used that variable to locate it. The 2.x line we use is a different implementation that `DllImport`s `e_sqlite3` directly.

Deferred out of 6.5.0 deliberately — the SQLite native unification already landed there and this is a separate, independently verifiable change.

### The three sites

| File | Value it sets |
|---|---|
| `Source/LinqToDB.LINQPad/DatabaseProviders/SQLiteProvider.cs` | `AppDomain.CurrentDomain.BaseDirectory` |
| `Tests/Linq/TestsInitialization.cs` | `AppDomain.CurrentDomain.BaseDirectory` |
| `Tests/Tests.T4/Shared.ttinclude` | the resolved `$(LinqToDBT4SharedTools)` path |

### Evidence gathered so far

Against `System.Data.SQLite` 2.0.4 and the rest of the restored SQLite closure:

- The string `PreLoadSQLite_BaseDirectory` does not appear in **any** of the three `System.Data.SQLite.dll` builds the package ships (`net471`, `netstandard2.0`, `netstandard2.1`), searched as both UTF-8 and UTF-16.
- `System.Data.SQLite` 2.0.4's nuspec declares **no package dependencies at all** — it is a self-contained managed assembly that P/Invokes `e_sqlite3`.
- Scanning every assembly in `SQLitePCLRaw.core`, `SQLitePCLRaw.provider.e_sqlite3`, `SQLitePCLRaw.provider.dynamic_cdecl`, `SQLitePCLRaw.bundle_e_sqlite3` and `Microsoft.Data.Sqlite.Core` finds no reference to it either.

So the variable is almost certainly dead configuration. It is *almost* rather than *certainly* because a negative from a corpus scan is not a negative about the running program — hence an experiment rather than a straight deletion.

### The experiment

Delete all three assignments, then verify by the paths that would actually break:

1. `Tests/Linq` SQLite fixture on **net462** and **net10.0**, across `SQLite.Classic` and `SQLite.MS`. net462 is the load-bearing one: the CLR does not probe `runtimes/<rid>/native/` on .NET Framework, so if anything still depends on being pointed at the native, that is where it shows.
2. A `Tests/Tests.T4` SQLite template run from Visual Studio. This is a genuinely different host — the T4 host is `devenv.exe`, whose base directory is not the tools folder, which is why this site passes an explicit path rather than `BaseDirectory`.
3. The LINQPad 5 `.lpx` and LINQPad 7+ driver SQLite smoke rows, since `SQLiteProvider.cs` sets it inside the driver.

Green on all three ⇒ delete. Red on any ⇒ record which host still needs it and keep just that site, with a comment saying what reads it.

### Out of scope: `SQLite.Runtime.props`

Removing that file was considered at the same time and **declined on evidence** — both of its targets are still load-bearing:

- The `CheckForAnyCPU` override shadows a target defined in `SQLitePCLRaw.lib.e_sqlite3` 3.53.3's `build/net471/SQLitePCLRaw.lib.e_sqlite3.props`. The LINQPad 5 driver builds AnyCPU on net472, so without the override the package's guard fails the build.
- The net462 hand-copy is required because the package's asset groups are `build: net471`, `lib: net471 + netstandard2.0`, `buildTransitive: net471/net8.0/net9.0` — there is no net462-compatible group, so a net462 project gets no natives from it at all.

Both narrow to the same condition: this stops being needed when linq2db drops net462 and the LINQPad 5 driver, not before.

ArgumentException "Property is not defined for type Nullable<T>" when a nullable struct built in an inner projection is read
issue.body:
### Description

When an inner projection (chained `Select`, `Concat`, `Distinct`, `OrderBy().Take()`, a `LEFT JOIN` subquery with `DefaultIfEmpty`, a scalar subquery with `FirstOrDefault`) constructs a struct lifted to `Nullable<T>`, `(T?)new T(...)`, and the outer query reads that member, query building throws `ArgumentException: Property 'Int32 Id' is not defined for type 'System.Nullable`1[T]'`. Reading it once is enough.

`SequenceHelper.CorrectTrackingPath` reaches the constructor through the `Convert(T -> T?)` with the member path typed `T?` (`m.Info`), then builds `Expression.MakeMemberAccess(m.Info, T.Id)` for each constructor parameter. `Id` is declared on `T`, not on `Nullable<T>`, so `Expression.Property` throws.

The same projection without the `(T?)` cast works, and so does a struct built with a member initializer (`(T?)new T { Id = ... }`), because the assignments loop skips members whose declaring type is not assignable from the path type. The parameters loop has no such check.

Found by the agentic review of #6069, under "Out-of-scope observations": https://github.com/linq2db/linq2db/pull/6069#pullrequestreview-5574646363

### Reproduction Steps

```cs
readonly record struct ParentPoint(int Id, int? Value);

// chained Select
db.Parent
	.Select(p => new { p.ParentID, Info = (ParentPoint?)new ParentPoint(p.ParentID, p.Value1) })
	.Select(m => new { m.ParentID, A = m.Info })
	.ToList();

// conditional null
db.Parent
	.Select(p => new { p.ParentID, Info = p.Value1 == null ? null : (ParentPoint?)new ParentPoint(p.ParentID, p.Value1) })
	.Select(m => new { m.ParentID, A = m.Info })
	.ToList();

// LEFT JOIN subquery
(from p in db.Parent
 from c in db.Child
	.Where(c => c.ParentID == p.ParentID)
	.Select(c => new { Info = (ParentPoint?)new ParentPoint(c.ChildID, c.ParentID) })
	.DefaultIfEmpty()
 select new { p.ParentID, A = c == null ? null : c.Info })
	.ToList();
```

issue.title: Negating a bool built from a nullable comparison drops rows where the value is NULL
issue.body:
### Summary

A `bool` member built from a nullable comparison in one projection and negated in a later filter loses the rows where the compared value is NULL. LINQ to Objects keeps them.

### Current behavior

With the test model's `Parent` (Parents 2 and 4 have a NULL `Value1`):

```cs
from x in db.Parent.Select(p => new { IsOne = p.Value1 == 1, p.ParentID })
where x.IsOne == false        // also: x.IsOne != true
select x.ParentID
```

generates, on every provider including SQLite:

```sql
SELECT [x].[ParentID] FROM [Parent] [x] WHERE [x].[Value1] <> 1
```

and returns 3, 5, 6 instead of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.

On providers without a boolean type (SQL Server, Oracle, Sybase), `where !x.IsOne` produces the same filter. So does a negated comparison against an aggregate (`IsLast = p.Children.Max(c => (int?)c.ChildID) == 11`, `where !x.IsLast`), and a negated column of a subquery used in a CROSS APPLY.

The filter reaches `SqlExpressionOptimizerVisitor` as an `IsTrue` predicate over the comparison, with the negation carried in `IsNot`:

- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/ExpressionBuildVisitor.cs:4906`: `x.IsOne == false` builds `IsTrue(..., isNot: true)`; `!x.IsOne` becomes the same after `Not` inverts the `IsTrue`.
- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/SqlProvider/SqlExpressionOptimizerVisitor.cs:138`: `VisitIsTruePredicate` visits the operand first, outside any NOT (`_isInsidePredicate` is false). `VisitNotPredicate` sets it for its operand at `:988`.
- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/SqlQuery/SqlPredicate.cs:485-487`: in that position, `ExprExpr.Reduce` drops the comparison's NULL guard (`Value1 = 1` with `UnknownAsValue` cleared).
- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/SqlQuery/SqlPredicate.cs:874-878`: `IsTrue.Reduce` then negates the already-reduced comparison, which gives `Value1 <> 1`.

### Expected behavior

The negation keeps C# semantics, e.g.

```sql
WHERE NOT ([x].[Value1] = 1 AND [x].[Value1] IS NOT NULL)
```

returning 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 on every provider.

### Notes

Reproduced against LINQ to Objects on SQLite.MS, SQLite.Classic and SQL Server 2022, direct and LinqService. For Oracle and Sybase, only the generated SQL was checked; the queries were not executed.

issue.title: Sql.Window: a constant window ORDER BY emits a bare integer index
issue.body:
### Summary

`Sql.Window`'s `OrderBy(object?)` accepts a constant and emits it verbatim into the `OVER (ORDER BY ...)` clause as a bare integer literal. SQL Server rejects the resulting query outright; SQLite, DuckDB and PostgreSQL accept it and sort by a constant, so every row ties and `ROW_NUMBER()` hands out an arbitrary, unstable numbering with no diagnostic anywhere.

### Background

The relevant declarations all take `object?`, and their documentation says *column*:

- `Source/LinqToDB/Sql/Sql.Window.cs:47` — `TThenPart OrderBy(object? orderBy)`, documented as "Adds an `ORDER BY column ASC` clause."
- `:49`, `:51`, `:53` — the `nulls` and `Desc` variants, same shape.

Nothing narrows the parameter to a column reference, and nothing rejects a constant.

### Current behavior

Verified at `75a837688` on .NET 10, direct contexts. The behaviour is pre-existing and not introduced by the PR that commit belongs to.

```csharp
from t in table
select new { RowNum = Sql.Window.RowNumber(w => w.OrderBy(1)) }
```

emits, on every provider tested:

```sql
SELECT
	ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY 1)
FROM
	[WindowFunctionTestEntity] [t]
```

| Provider | Outcome |
|---|---|
| SqlServer.2022.MS | `SqlException` 5308 — "Windowed functions, aggregates and NEXT VALUE FOR functions do not support integer indices as ORDER BY clause expressions." |
| PostgreSQL.17 | accepted, constant sort key |
| DuckDB | accepted, constant sort key |
| SQLite.MS | accepted, constant sort key |

The literal is evaluated as a **constant expression, not an ordinal**: `OrderBy(2)` against a single-column projection also succeeds on PostgreSQL, DuckDB and SQLite, which an ordinal reading would have to reject. So on those three the window ends up with no effective ordering.

### Expected behavior

A constant window ordering should not reach the server as a bare integer. Either:

- reject it at translation time with a clear message — the ordering cannot be honoured, and the API already documents the parameter as a column; or
- lower it to the provider's legal form for "no meaningful ordering", which T-SQL spells `ORDER BY (SELECT 1)`.

Rejecting at translation looks like the more consistent option. The accepted-but-constant behaviour on the other three providers is not useful either, so silently differing per provider is the worst of the available outcomes.

### Notes

- Providers not covered: Oracle, DB2, MySQL/MariaDB, Firebird, SAP HANA, ClickHouse, Sybase, Informix, YDB. Only the four above were exercised; SQL Server is the only one of those that errors.
- Not checked: whether the legacy `Sql.Ext()...Over().OrderBy(...)` analytic-functions API behaves the same way, and whether `OrderBy(Sql.AsSql(1))` lowers differently. #5782 records `Sql.AsSql` as an effective escape hatch for a constant *argument* (`Count(Sql.AsSql(1), ...)`), so it may serve here too.
- Surfaced while reviewing #5783. `RowNumber(w => w.OrderBy(1))` is listed in that PR's description as one of the shapes its `[ServerSideOnly]` change fixes, and was considered for its regression test; it was left out once this came to light, because covering it would require `[ThrowsForProvider]` for every SQL Server version.

issue.title: Arithmetic between value-converted columns adds the stored numbers even when the converters disagree
issue.body:
Arithmetic between two columns that carry hand-written value converters adds the stored numbers without checking that the converters agree on what those numbers mean. A column counting seconds and one counting ticks are summed as if they counted the same thing, and the answer comes back wrong rather than refused.

Verified on `900d8bd0c4` with no library changes.

### Repro

```csharp
[Table]
sealed class Row
{
    [PrimaryKey] public int Id { get; set; }

    [Column(DataType = DataType.Int64)] public TimeSpan InTicks   { get; set; }
    [Column(DataType = DataType.Int64)] public TimeSpan InSeconds { get; set; }
}

var ms = new MappingSchema();

new FluentMappingBuilder(ms)
    .Entity<Row>()
        .Property(e => e.InTicks)
            .HasConversion(ts => ts.Ticks, v => TimeSpan.FromTicks(v))
        .Property(e => e.InSeconds)
            .HasConversion(ts => ts.Ticks / TimeSpan.TicksPerSecond, v => TimeSpan.FromTicks(v * TimeSpan.TicksPerSecond))
    .Build();

// one row, both columns holding 90 minutes
t.Select(r => r.InTicks + r.InSeconds).Single();
```

| Expression | Expected | Actual |
|---|---|---|
| `InTicks + InSeconds` | `03:00:00` | `01:30:00.0005400` |
| `InTicks + InTicks` | `03:00:00` | `03:00:00` |
| `InTicks + InSeconds` without `Sql.AsSql` | `03:00:00` | `01:30:00.0005400` |

The wrong value is 90 minutes plus 5400 **ticks** - the seconds column's stored `5400` added as if it were a tick count. Wrong by a factor of ten million, and silent.

Not specific to `TimeSpan`. The same shape applies to any two columns of one CLR type whose converters disagree about what the stored number represents; `TimeSpan` only makes it easy to see, because the error is a plausible-looking duration rather than a garbage value.

### Expected

Either a refusal naming the mismatch, or the two operands brought onto common terms before they are added. A refusal is the safer of the two: only the converters know what their numbers mean, and nothing in the model states it.

### Notes

#5750 adds `[Duration(DurationUnit)]`, which declares what a duration column's number counts, and reconciles the operands wherever both sides declare it. It also refuses the mixed case - one side declared, the other only converted - in `bed2222fe0`.

This issue is the remaining half: neither side declares, which is what every value-converted column looks like today. It predates that PR and is unchanged by it.

issue.title: Union and Intersect of an optional object against a `(T?)null` branch throw "Could not decide which construction type to use"
issue.body:
### Description

A set operation throws when one branch projects an object that may be missing, and the other branch projects `(T?)null` in the same place. The object comes from the builder itself, which decides whether it is there by testing one of its columns for NULL:

- an entity from a `DefaultIfEmpty()` join,
- a nullable association,
- a `FirstOrDefault()` subquery.

`Union` and `Intersect` throw for every one of these, with either branch first. `Concat` works in both orders, and so does `Except` with the object branch first.

`Except` with the null branch first doesn't throw, but `nulls.Except(joined)` returns 0 rows where 1 is correct. That looks like a separate problem and is not covered here.

### Reproduction Steps

```cs
[Table]
public class Parent
{
	[PrimaryKey] public int ParentID { get; set; }

	[Association(ThisKey = nameof(ParentID), OtherKey = nameof(Child.ParentID), CanBeNull = true)]
	public Child? FirstChild { get; set; }
}

[Table]
public class Child
{
	[PrimaryKey] public int ChildID  { get; set; }
	[Column]     public int ParentID { get; set; }
}

var joined =
	from p in db.GetTable<Parent>()
	from c in db.GetTable<Child>().Where(c => c.ParentID == p.ParentID).DefaultIfEmpty()
	select new { p.ParentID, Child = c };

var association = db.GetTable<Parent>()
	.Select(p => new { p.ParentID, Child = p.FirstChild });

var firstOrDefault = db.GetTable<Parent>()
	.Select(p => new
	{
		p.ParentID,
		Child = db.GetTable<Child>()
			.Where(c => c.ParentID == p.ParentID)
			.OrderBy(c => c.ChildID)
			.FirstOrDefault(),
	});

var nulls = db.GetTable<Parent>()
	.Select(p => new { p.ParentID, Child = (Child?)null });

joined.Union(nulls).ToList();          // throws
joined.Intersect(nulls).ToList();      // throws
association.Union(nulls).ToList();     // throws
association.Intersect(nulls).ToList(); // throws
firstOrDefault.Union(nulls).ToList();  // throws
nulls.Union(joined).ToList();          // throws, same with the branches swapped

joined.Concat(nulls).ToList();         // works
```

### Exception details

```
LinqToDB.LinqToDBException: Could not decide which construction type to use `query.Select(x => new <>f__AnonymousType0`2 { ... })` to specify projection.
   at LinqToDB.Internal.Linq.Builder.SetOperationBuilder.SetOperationContext.MergeProjections(Expression path, Expression projection1, Expression projection2, ProjectFlags flags) in /_/Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/SetOperationBuilder.cs:line 438
   at LinqToDB.Internal.Linq.Builder.SetOperationBuilder.SetOperationContext.MakeExpression(Expression path, ProjectFlags flags) in /_/Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/SetOperationBuilder.cs:line 274
   at LinqToDB.Internal.Linq.Builder.ExpressionBuildVisitor.MakeWithCache(IBuildContext context, Expression expression) in /_/Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/ExpressionBuildVisitor.cs:line 520
   at LinqToDB.Internal.Linq.Builder.ExpressionBuildVisitor.VisitContextRefExpression(ContextRefExpression node) in /_/Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/ExpressionBuildVisitor.cs:line 3287
   ...
   at LinqToDB.Internal.Linq.Builder.SetOperationBuilder.BuildMethodCall(ExpressionBuilder builder, MethodCallExpression methodCall, BuildInfo buildInfo) in /_/Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/SetOperationBuilder.cs:line 70
```

### Regression?

Partly. In 5.4.1 the `DefaultIfEmpty()` join worked with the object branch first:
- `joined.Union(nulls)` returned 3 rows and `joined.Intersect(nulls)` returned 1, both correct.
- With the null branch first, every set operation threw "Types in UNION are constructed incompatibly", `Concat` included.

In 6.5.1, `Concat` works in both orders, while `Union` and `Intersect` throw in both orders. 6.0.0, 6.2.1 and 6.4.0 throw the same way for the object-first `Union` and `Intersect`.

The other two shapes failed differently in 5.4.1:
- the association with "Associations with Concat/Union or other Set operations are not supported";
- `FirstOrDefault()` with SQLite's "sub-select returns 2 columns - expected 1".

### Linq To DB version

6.5.1

10.0

macOS

issue.title: Sybase: SybaseTools.GetDataProvider ignores the requested SybaseProvider (regression from #5228)
issue.body:
### Summary

`SybaseTools.GetDataProvider(SybaseProvider.Unmanaged)` (and the other `SybaseProvider` arguments) is ignored: the detector re-detects the provider from scratch, so an explicitly requested native provider comes back as the managed one when `Sybase.AdoNet45.AseClient` is not present. Regression from #5228, shipped since 6.0.0.

### Current behavior

- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/DataProvider/Sybase/SybaseProviderDetector.cs:43-51` — `GetDataProvider(ConnectionOptions options, SybaseProvider provider, NoDialect version)` starts with `provider = DetectProvider(options, SybaseProvider.AutoDetect);`, discarding the argument.
- `SybaseProviderDetector.cs:59-62` — `DetectProvider(options, provider)` already returns an explicit `DataAction` / `Unmanaged` unchanged; passing `AutoDetect` skips that, and the result falls through to assembly presence (`:83-85`).
- Every other detector passes the argument through: `ProviderDetectorBase.cs:78`, `ClickHouseProviderDetector.cs:38`, `MySqlProviderDetector.cs:94`, `SqlServerProviderDetector.cs:122`, `InformixProviderDetector.cs:52`, `SQLiteProviderDetector.cs:55`, `OracleProviderDetector.cs:78`, `AccessProviderDetector.cs:71`, `SapHanaProviderDetector.cs:51`.

Introduced by `00a2ac6d5` (#5228, 2025-12-04), which replaced

```cs
if (provider == SybaseProvider.AutoDetect)
	provider = DetectProvider();
```

with the unconditional re-detection; `git tag --contains 00a2ac6d5` lists v6.0.0 through v6.5.1.

Observed 2026-10-27 on .NET 10 without the native assembly: `SybaseTools.GetDataProvider(SybaseProvider.Unmanaged).Name` is `Sybase.Managed`, where `Sybase` is expected.

### Expected behavior

An explicit `SybaseProvider.DataAction` or `SybaseProvider.Unmanaged` selects that provider, as for every other provider family; only `AutoDetect` is detected:

```cs
provider = DetectProvider(options, provider);
```

### Notes

- The opposite direction (an explicit `DataAction` returning the native provider when the native assembly is present) follows from the same line but was not measured.
- The provider-name path is unaffected: `"Sybase.Native"` / `ProviderName.SybaseManaged` resolve through `DetectProvider(ConnectionOptions)` (`SybaseProviderDetector.cs:20-26`).
- Found by the #5159 WASM harness, whose provider-matrix check compares each row's constructed provider with the one it names; the native Sybase row works around this through `"Sybase.Native"`.

issue.title: KeyedQuery eager loading applies a detail-side Take/Skip globally instead of per parent
issue.body:
### Summary

Under the `KeyedQuery` eager-loading strategy, a `Take` / `Skip` on an eager-loaded child collection is applied once to the whole child query instead of once per parent key. The first parent consumes the entire limit and every subsequent parent gets an empty collection, with no error. The `Default` strategy handles the same query correctly.

### Current behavior

With two parents that each have three children, and a detail sequence limited to two rows:

```cs
db.GetTable<Item>()
    .OrderBy(i => i.Id)
    .Select(i => new
    {
        i.Value,
        Logs = i.Logs.OrderBy(l => l.Id).Take(2).Select(l => new { l.Log }).ToArray(),
    })
    .ToArray();
```

the per-parent child counts come back as `[2, 0]` where `[2, 2]` is expected. The child query carries a single global limit:

```sql
SELECT
	[l].[ItemId],
	[l].[Log]
FROM
	[ItemLog] [l]
WHERE
	[l].[ItemId] IN (1, 2)
ORDER BY
	[l].[Id]
LIMIT @take   -- 2
```

Two rows are fetched for the whole batch, both belong to item 1, and item 2 is left with an empty collection.

- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/ExpressionBuilder.EagerLoadKeyedQuery.cs:203-223` — the `canUseContains` path rewrites the child's correlation predicate, replacing `childFK == parentKey` with `keys.Contains(childFK)`. Only the equality is transformed; the rest of the detail sequence, including the `Take`, is carried over unchanged and therefore ends up scoped to the combined result set rather than to one parent.
- The same file contains no limit-handling logic at all — a search for `Take`, `Skip`, `Limited` and `RowNumber` across it matches twice, both times the word "Skip" inside the comment `// Skip child query when there are no parent keys` at `:954` and `:978`.
- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/Linq/Builder/ExpressionBuilder.EagerLoad.cs:536-549` — `ResolveStrategy` routes on CTE / window-function support only, so a limited child does not cause a fallback to a strategy that can express the limit, and `EagerLoadFallbackReason` has no member for this case.

The `Default` strategy emits a `CROSS APPLY` / `LATERAL` subquery per parent, which scopes the limit correctly and returns `[2, 2]` for the query above.

### Expected behavior

A `Take` / `Skip` on an eager-loaded child collection applies per parent key under every strategy, matching the `Default` strategy and the in-memory semantics of the same LINQ expression. If `KeyedQuery` cannot express a per-key limit, the strategy resolver should fall back to one that can rather than silently returning wrong rows.

### Notes

Reproduced on `SQLite.Classic` and `PostgreSQL.18`, in both direct and remote (`LinqService`) contexts — `[2, 0]` in all four. The SQL above is the SQLite form; PostgreSQL emits the same shape.

The root cause is stated from reading the rewrite at `:203-223` together with the emitted SQL; the wrong result and the generated query are both confirmed empirically, while the attribution to that specific rewrite is a reading of the code rather than a bisect.

Found while fixing #5935, which is a separate defect in the same area (an eager-loaded `OrderBy` whose key is absent from the projection threw `InvalidOperationException`). That fix does not touch this behaviour.

issue.title: SQL Server before 2016: reach elapsed time through the shared decomposition
issue.body:
### Summary

Elapsed-time lowering is gated at SQL Server 2016, where `DATEDIFF_BIG` arrives, so `(a - b).Total*` is refused on 2005-2014. The shared decomposition that SQL CE and Sybase use needs no 64-bit difference function and would reach those versions, which would leave SQL Server 2014 no weaker than SQL CE.

### Background

#5750 replaced the old rewrite of `(a - b).TotalDays|TotalHours|TotalMinutes|TotalSeconds|TotalMilliseconds` into `Sql.DateDiff(part, b, a)` with real elapsed lowering. That rewrite counted boundary crossings rather than elapsed time, so it was silently wrong for unaligned inputs — 10:59 to 11:01 answered two minutes.

Removing it is right, and where the value is projected the query falls back to .NET and is exact. What changed on 2005-2014 is that a `WHERE`, `ORDER BY` or aggregate position now refuses instead of answering approximately.

### Current behavior

`SqlServerSqlExpressionConvertVisitor` hardcodes `DateDiff_Big` in `CountDateBoundaries` and gates the feature at 2016, so 2005-2014 refuses.

SQL CE and Sybase reach an elapsed difference through the shared `CountDateBoundaries` + `ShiftDate` decomposition instead, which anchors in days and measures the remainder over a sub-day window — at millisecond resolution that is at most 86,400,000, comfortably inside a 32-bit `DATEDIFF`.

Eleven pre-existing tests are marked `[ThrowsCannotBeConverted(TestProvName.AllSqlServer2014Minus)]` as a result, across `DateTimeFunctionsTests`, `DateTimeOffsetTests` and `DateOnlyFunctionTests`.

### Expected behavior

The decomposition is used below 2016 the way it is for the other providers without a 64-bit difference, and those eleven gates come off. `FinestDateUnit` on that visitor is already version-aware, so the shape for extending it exists.

### Notes

Raised in review of #5750 and deliberately not done there — it is new provider work rather than a defect in that change, and the versions in question are no worse off than before it in any position where an answer was previously correct.

issue.title: PostgreSQL: filtered aggregates emit a FILTER clause on 9.2/9.3, where it is a syntax error
issue.body:
### Summary

A filtered aggregate (`g.Where(…).Sum(…)`) is emitted with an SQL `FILTER (WHERE …)` clause on PostgreSQL 9.2 and 9.3, which those versions cannot parse — `FILTER` arrived in PostgreSQL 9.4.

### Background

linq2db models the aggregate `FILTER` clause as a provider capability, `AggregateFunctionsMemberTranslatorBase.IsFilterSupported`, which defaults to `false`. When it is not set, the aggregate is emulated with a conditional expression instead, so the capability flag is the only thing standing between a provider and unparseable SQL.

### Current behavior

- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/DataProvider/PostgreSQL/Translation/PostgreSQLMemberTranslator.cs:370` — `protected override bool IsFilterSupported => true;`, with no version condition.
- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/DataProvider/PostgreSQL/PostgreSQLDataProvider.cs:103-110` — versioned member translators are selected from `v95` upward (`v19`, `v18`, `v13`, `v11`, `v95`); everything below falls to the default arm `_ => new PostgreSQLMemberTranslator()`. So `v92` and `v93` receive the translator that claims `FILTER` support.
- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/DataProvider/PostgreSQL/PostgreSQLProviderDetector.cs:131-132` — `{ Major: > 9 } or { Major: 9, Minor: > 4 } => PostgreSQLVersion.v95`, `{ Major: 9, Minor: > 2 } => PostgreSQLVersion.v93`. A genuine 9.4 server is therefore detected as `v93` as well.
- `Source/LinqToDB/Internal/DataProvider/Translation/AggregateFunctionsMemberTranslatorBase.cs:19,122,139,298` — the flag's default and its three consumers. When it is false the emitted form is `SUM(CASE WHEN … THEN … ELSE NULL END)` / `COUNT(CASE WHEN … THEN 1 ELSE NULL END)`, which every supported PostgreSQL version parses.

The effect surfaces as test exclusions rather than as bug reports. 37 tests exclude `TestProvName.AllPostgreSQL93Minus` with the comment `// PostgreSQL 9.4+ (FILTER clause)`:

- `Tests/Linq/Linq/GroupByTests.cs` — 22
- `Tests/Linq/Linq/CountTests.cs` — 11
- `Tests/Linq/Linq/StringJoinTests.cs` — 2
- `Tests/Linq/Linq/BooleanTests.cs` — 1
- `Tests/Linq/UserTests/Issue1564Tests.cs` — 1

### Expected behavior

Versions that predate the clause should take the existing emulation rather than emitting `FILTER`.

The natural boundary is the **9.5 tier**, not 9.4: `PostgreSQLVersion` has no `v94` member, and the detector maps a 9.4 server to `v93`. The 9.5 tier already exists for exactly this feature — `PostgreSQL95MemberTranslator` is already the dispatch target, and `PostgreSQL95WindowFunctionsMemberTranslator.IsWindowFilterSupported => true` already gates the window-function counterpart the same way.

Shape of the fix:

- `PostgreSQLMemberTranslator`'s `IsFilterSupported` override becomes `false` (the override itself is tracked in `PublicAPI.Shipped.txt` and should be kept rather than removed).
- `PostgreSQL95MemberTranslator` overrides `CreateAggregateFunctionsMemberTranslator()` with a nested subclass returning `true`.
- No change to `PostgreSQLDataProvider` is needed — `>= PostgreSQLVersion.v95 => new PostgreSQL95MemberTranslator()` already exists.

A genuine 9.4 server then uses the emulation. That is conservative but correct, and avoiding it means adding a `v94` enum member with its detector arm and provider instance, which is a larger change.

The conservative arm catches more than a genuine 9.4 server. `PostgreSQLProviderDetector.cs:10` passes `PostgreSQLVersion.v92` as `DefaultVersion`, and that value is what gets used when auto-detection is disabled (`:98`), when `DetectServerVersion` returns null (`:108`), and as the fallback arm of the version map (`:133`). Any such context emits `FILTER` today — valid against whatever server it is in fact talking to, which in practice is a modern one — and takes the emulation once the gate is in place. Results are identical either way and the direction is safe, but it is a SQL-shape change for a wider population than the 9.2/9.3 range alone suggests, so it is worth stating rather than discovering. Whether `DefaultVersion` should stay pinned at the oldest dialect is a separate question and not in scope here.

Once gated, the 37 exclusions listed above become removable, which is the natural regression test for the fix.

### Notes

- A second `FILTER` emitter is not covered by this flag. `PostgreSQLMemberTranslator.StringMemberTranslator.TranslateStringJoin` passes `filter:` unconditionally and belongs to a different nested class, so string aggregates over a filtered grouping remain broken on 9.2/9.3 until the same tier split is applied there. The two `StringJoinTests` exclusions above are that path, and they should stay excluded until it is.
- Window functions use a separate capability, `IsWindowFilterSupported`, already tiered at 9.5. It is a distinct concept from the grouped-aggregate flag and is not affected.
- **Reproduced since filing.** This note originally recorded the syntax error as inferred rather than observed. It has since been confirmed against live 9.2 and 9.3 servers while the fix was being proven before its port to PR #5949: `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...)` is rejected with `42601: syntax error at or near "("`, and with the gate applied 777 tests across `GroupByTests`, `CountTests` and `BooleanTests` pass on both versions while PostgreSQL 19 still emits a real `FILTER` clause. The 777-test half is independently reproduced by CI on #5949, which is green with those exclusions removed.
